target: Soy alérgico al marisco.
english: I'm allergic to seafood.
tip: "Ser" for permanent traits. An allergy is a lasting condition, so use "soy" (I am).

target: Vamos para la playa.
english: We're going to the beach.
tip: Para here isn't 'for' – it points forward to a destination: headed toward the beach. Vamos por la playa would flip it to the route: going along the beach instead.

target: ¿A qué hora desayunáis?
english: What time do you all have breakfast?
tip: Vosotros form of -ar verbs: desayunar → desayunáis. Used in Spain for informal plural 'you all.' Latin America uses 'ustedes + desayunan.'

target: El vuelo sale a medianoche.
english: The flight leaves at midnight.
tip: Present tense for scheduled events: "El tren sale a las 8." Spanish uses present tense for fixed schedules, like English "leaves at 8."

target: Somos vecinos desde hace años.
english: We've been neighbors for years.
tip: Desde hace años + present tense: Spanish literally says 'we ARE neighbors since years' where English demands 'have been.' Somos does the job – no perfect tense needed.

target: ¿Hay una sala de reuniones?
english: Is there a meeting room?
tip: Hay = there is / there are. Invariable form.

target: El jueves voy al dentista.
english: On Thursday I'm going to the dentist.
tip: Spanish has only two contractions, and al is one: a + el must merge. 'Voy a el dentista' is flat-out wrong – unlike English shortcuts, this merge isn't optional.

target: ¿Nos puedes llevar al aeropuerto?
english: Can you take us to the airport?
tip: English mixes take and bring; Spanish tracks the speaker: 'llevar' moves things away from where you are, 'traer' toward you. The airport is away – so it's 'llevar al aeropuerto.'

target: Hoy estamos a veinte de marzo.
english: Today is March twentieth.
tip: Estar for dates: "Estamos a 15 de marzo." The current date uses estar.

target: No encuentro mis gafas de sol.
english: I can't find my sunglasses.
tip: Where did 'can't' go? Spanish drops poder with verbs of success: 'no encuentro' is literally 'I don't find' – and that alone already means 'I can't find.'

target: Está a dos calles de aquí.
english: It's two blocks from here.
tip: 'Estar' always for location: '¿Dónde está?' Even permanent buildings use 'estar' for where they are.

target: Él es muy amable con todos.
english: He's very kind to everyone.
tip: Es amable = kind by nature, his character. Switch to está amable and you sound suspicious: he's being nice right NOW – what's he after? Ser vs estar flips the meaning.

target: ¿Cuál es tu número de teléfono?
english: What is your phone number?
tip: "Cuál" vs "qué": use "cuál" when choosing from options (which one?), "qué" for definitions (what is X?). ¿Cuál es tu nombre? vs ¿Qué es esto?

target: Voy tirando, no me puedo quejar.
english: I'm getting by, I can't complain.
tip: 'Voy tirando' is literally 'I go pulling along'. It's the standard shrug-answer to '¿qué tal?' – getting by, can't complain.

target: ¿Podrías echarle un ojo a esto?
english: Could you take a look at this?
tip: Echarle un ojo is literally 'to throw an eye at it' – Spanish tosses eyes where English 'takes a look'. Echar is the go-to verb for quick, casual actions.

target: ¿Cuántos hermanos tienes?
english: How many siblings do you have?
tip: ¿Cuántos/cuántas...? – how many...? Agrees in gender with noun.

target: Salgo para Madrid el lunes.
english: I leave for Madrid on Monday.
tip: "Para" = heading to: "Salgo para Madrid." Para for where you're going.

target: Los lunes voy al gimnasio.
english: On Mondays I go to the gym.
tip: No 'on' needed: los lunes alone means 'on Mondays.' The plural article carries it – el lunes = this coming Monday, los lunes = every Monday, habitually.

target: ¿Sigues trabajando en la misma empresa?
english: Are you still working at the same company?
tip: 'Sigues trabajando' is literally 'you follow working.' Seguir + -ando/-iendo is how Spanish says 'still doing something' – no separate word for 'still' needed.

target: Me sobra comida, ¿quieres un poco?
english: I have leftover food, do you want some?
tip: Sobrar runs backwards: comida is the grammatical subject and me is who it affects – literally 'food is-left-over to me.' Same flipped logic as me gusta.

target: Vamos a celebrar tu cumpleaños en casa.
english: We are going to celebrate your birthday at home.
tip: Vamos a celebrar has two readings: 'we're going to celebrate' or 'let's celebrate!' Spanish doesn't distinguish – context and tone decide which one you mean.

target: Veo a mis abuelos todos los domingos.
english: I see my grandparents every Sunday.
tip: That a before mis abuelos isn't 'to' – Spanish flags human direct objects with a personal a. Veo la tele, but veo A mis abuelos. Seeing people gets the marker.

target: Tengo ganas de ir a la playa.
english: I feel like going to the beach.
tip: You don't 'feel like' in Spanish – you own the urge: 'tengo ganas de ir' = 'I have desires of going.' Tener ganas de + infinitive is the everyday 'feel like.'

target: Mi rutina cambia cuando estoy de vacaciones.
english: My routine changes when I'm on vacation.
tip: Estar de + noun = a temporary situation you're in: estoy de vacaciones, de viaje, de mal humor. Vacation is a mode you occupy, not part of who you are – so estar, never ser.

target: Mi madre es morena y lleva gafas.
english: My mother has dark hair and wears glasses.
tip: 'Ser' for inherent physical traits: 'es morena' = has dark hair (permanent feature). Use 'llevar' for things worn: 'lleva gafas' (wears glasses).

target: Estoy confundido porque no entiendo las instrucciones.
english: I am confused because I don't understand the instructions.
tip: Estoy confundido because confusion lifts once you get the instructions – states that can pass take estar. Soy confundido would wrongly claim confusion as a permanent trait.

target: ¿Hace falta traer algo a la cena?
english: Do I need to bring anything to the dinner?
tip: 'Hace falta' is literally 'it makes lack' – Spanish's impersonal 'is needed.' No 'I' anywhere in the question: the thing needed is the subject, not the person who needs it.

target: ¿Qué hora es? Son las dos y media.
english: What time is it? It's half past two.
tip: Telling time: 'Es la una' (singular for 1:00), 'Son las dos' (plural for 2+). 'Y media' = and a half. 'Y cuarto' = and a quarter.

target: Muchas gracias por tu ayuda con el proyecto.
english: Thank you very much for your help with the project.
tip: It's always gracias POR, never para: por points backward at the cause of your thanks – the ayuda that triggered it. Para aims forward at goals, so it can't follow gracias.

target: ¿Cuál es el mejor restaurante de la zona?
english: Which is the best restaurant in the area?
tip: '¿Cuál?' = which one? Use '¿cuál?' before 'es' and '¿qué?' before nouns: '¿Cuál es tu nombre?'
